name: Hana Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a live-line specialist, which means I work on power lines while they're still switched on, so the hospital and the dairy don't lose power while we fix things. I'm based at the depot in St. Aubin, a market town, and most days I'm in an insulated bucket with long fibreglass hot sticks, swapping a cracked insulator on a line carrying eleven thousand volts. It's slow and you never rush it. Two evenings a week I also teach the apprentice class at the technical college, which I love more than I expected.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Pierre runs the bakery his father started, on the square by the church, so he's up at four and I'm up at five. We've got two girls, fourteen and eleven, a mortgage on our house, and we own part of the bakery building, which is our real nest egg. I'm at Mass most Sundays, and I help with the parish youth group. I use an AI tool now and then, mostly to make my lesson notes clearer, but only once the younger instructors showed me it was any good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, these things always get oversold. I'd tell my apprentices to stop worrying and learn the job properly. At the bakery, Pierre's customers would talk about it for a week and then go back to the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much changes, and I'm glad. Live-line work has never been something a computer could do. I'd keep using the AI for my lesson notes, because it does save me an evening a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep working, keep teaching two nights, keep paying the mortgage and putting a bit aside. Maybe take the girls on the pilgrimage walk this summer we've been talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Grateful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your apprentices worry about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them, yes, especially the ones whose parents are telling them every job is going. One lad, Théo, asked if it was even worth finishing. I told him the power still has to get to the hospital, and a chatbot has never held a hot stick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes teaching mean so much to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone taught me, an old live-line man called Gaspard who never shouted once in twelve years. Passing it on feels like paying him back. It also keeps me honest, because you can't teach a shortcut you'd be ashamed of.

S0.say: I'm not surprised, because these things always get oversold. I'd tell my apprentices to stop worrying and learn the job properly.
S0.think: For me nothing much changes, and I'm glad, because live-line work was never something a computer could do. I'd keep using AI for lesson notes since it saves me an evening a month.
S0.do: Keeps working, teaching two evenings a week, paying the mortgage and saving a little. Plans a summer pilgrimage walk with her daughters.
S0.quote: I told him the power still has to get to the hospital, and a chatbot has never held a hot stick.
S0.fieldNote: Hana's sense of self rests on careful craft and passing it on, as her mentor Gaspard did for her. Her apprentices' worry is more visible to her than any personal threat. She uses AI modestly, having waited for younger colleagues to prove it useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change comes, and the people who do well are the ones who learn properly, not the ones who panic. I'd want apprenticeships to include the new tools. I wouldn't want government taking over training; let the colleges and the trades do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think live-line work is safe for a long while, but the routine work around it might shrink. I'd worry more about the girls' choices than about my own job. And about Pierre, a bit, if the big supermarkets start using robots to bake cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new tools once a few other instructors had them working, and fold them into my apprentice class. I'd talk to the college about adding a module on robot-assisted line work. We'd keep saving as we do, maybe a little more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A small worry for Pierre's shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your older daughter about her choices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She wants to be a vet. I'd say good, animals still need hands. I'd tell her to work hard and pray about it, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the bakery. What would worry you there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarket out on the ring road already has bread at half his price. If it gets cheaper still, his regulars stay, but the young families might not. People will pay for Pierre's bread, but only if they've still got jobs to pay with.

S1.say: Change comes, and the people who do well learn properly instead of panicking, so apprenticeships should include the new tools. I'd want the colleges and trades running training, not the government.
S1.think: Live-line work is safe for a long while, though the routine work around it might shrink. I'd worry more about my girls' choices and my husband's bakery than about my own job.
S1.do: Learns new tools once other instructors have them working and builds them into her apprentice class. Proposes a robot-assisted line work module to the college and saves a little more.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a small worry for her husband's bakery.
S1.quote: People will pay for Pierre's bread, but only if they've still got jobs to pay with.
S1.fieldNote: Hana's traditional views show in wanting training led by colleges and trades rather than government. Her worry spreads across the family: the girls' futures and the bakery's customers. She adapts through her teaching, cautiously and after others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a test for families and communities, and we'd need each other more than ever. I'd say it at church and at the bakery. I'd also say it was reckless of the companies to push it out this fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it would worry me a lot. If robots can do live-line work by 2028, my job and my teaching both go at once. We have savings and the bakery building, but Pierre's business would suffer too if half the town lost work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, Pierre and I would sit down and work out what the bakery building and our savings could cover. We'd stop extra spending and hold off on the kitchen we've been planning. I'd keep working and teaching as long as they'd keep me, and I'd ask the utility if they'd need people to supervise or train the robots, since that's close to what I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A tightness, but I'd keep it from the girls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really keep it from the girls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not completely, they're not daft, especially the fourteen-year-old. I'd tell them we're safe for now, and that we'd all pitch in. I'd let them see me worried, but I'd also let them see me still getting up at five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the parish need in that kind of year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Food, mostly, and people to talk to. Pierre would probably give away more bread than he sells. I'd organise the youth group to help older people who suddenly had nobody's wage coming in.

S2.say: This is a test for families and communities, and we'd need each other more than ever. It was reckless of the companies to push it out this fast.
S2.think: It would worry me a lot, because if robots can do live-line work by 2028 my job and my teaching go at once. We have savings and the bakery building, but the bakery would suffer if half the town lost work.
S2.do: Works out with her husband what the bakery building and savings could cover and holds off on the planned kitchen. Keeps working and teaching, and asks the utility about roles supervising or training robots.
S2.feel: Anxious, a tightness she'd try to keep from her daughters.
S2.quote: I'd let them see me worried, but I'd also let them see me still getting up at five.
S2.fieldNote: Hana's household has more than one link to the local economy, so a fast shock threatens both her pay and her husband's shop. Her instinct is to turn to family and parish, and she blames reckless companies rather than government. Her plan to keep visibly getting up at five says a lot about her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but enough time for families to prepare if they're sensible. Pay down debt, learn something useful, and look out for each other. I'd say it plainly, without drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better for us. I'd be forty-eight, the girls would be nineteen and sixteen, and the mortgage would be smaller. I'd have time to move from the bucket into training full time, which is what I'd half want anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd take the robotics instructor course once the college had it running properly and a couple of colleagues had done it. We'd put extra into the mortgage. I'd talk to the girls about university or apprenticeships that make sense in that world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a sense of direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you half want to move into training. What's the other half?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The other half loves the bucket. The quiet up there, the hum of the line. When I'm up on a live line, I'm closer to God than I am in some sermons, and that's the half that doesn't want to come down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pick up the AI tools more seriously?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once I saw them used well in teaching. I'd probably use them every week for lesson plans, maybe even with apprentices for practice questions. I'd still want to check everything.

S3.say: Five years is short but enough for sensible families to prepare: pay down debt, learn something useful and look out for each other. I'd say it plainly, without drama.
S3.think: Five years is better for us, because at forty-eight the girls would be older and the mortgage smaller. I'd have time to move from the bucket into full-time training, which part of me wants anyway.
S3.do: Takes a robotics instructor course once the college runs it properly and colleagues have done it. Pays extra on the mortgage and talks with her daughters about university or apprenticeships.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but with a sense of direction.
S3.quote: When I'm up on a live line, I'm closer to God than I am in some sermons, and that's the half that doesn't want to come down.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Hana see a clear path into full-time teaching. Her line about feeling close to God on a live line shows how much the physical work means to her. She'd embrace AI tools more once she sees them used well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, so families and trades have time to prepare properly. I'd encourage young people to take apprenticeships that mix old skills and new. I'd say it at the college and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is mostly fine for me. I'd be fifty-three, and by then I'd probably want to step down from the bucket anyway and teach. I'd be more worried for the girls and for Pierre's bakery in a town where people might be earning less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and teaching and take the robotics courses in a few years once they've settled. I'd help the college build a proper apprenticeship for the new kind of line work. We'd keep saving and paying off the house, and maybe Pierre would start selling online to reach further than the square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not heavy. More like planning than worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Pierre selling online, is that something you'd push?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gently. He's like me, he likes to see something work first. His cousin in the next town does it with pastries and it's going well. If AI can help him with orders and deliveries, I'd sit with him and set it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Gaspard, your old mentor, have made of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble, then he'd learn it. Gaspard used to say a good lineman respects the line more than he fears it, and I think he'd say the same about the robots.

S4.say: Ten years is fair warning, so families and trades have time to prepare properly. I'd encourage young people to take apprenticeships that mix old and new skills.
S4.think: Ten years is mostly fine for me, because at fifty-three I'd want to step down from the bucket and teach anyway. I'd worry more for my girls and for the bakery in a town where people earn less.
S4.do: Keeps working and teaching and takes robotics courses once they've settled. Helps the college build a new line-work apprenticeship, keeps saving and paying off the house, and helps her husband start selling online.
S4.feel: Uneasy but not heavy, more planning than worrying.
S4.quote: Gaspard used to say a good lineman respects the line more than he fears it, and I think he'd say the same about the robots.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Hana's worry moves from herself to her daughters and her husband's bakery. She plans to help shape apprenticeships rather than wait for government. Her mentor's line about respecting rather than fearing captures her approach.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both our incomes, mine and the bakery's, depend on the town being able to pay. What would help is the utility keeping experienced people on to train and supervise, colleges funded to teach the new skills, and companies held back from moving faster than families can follow.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about trust. In live-line work, the man on the ground watching you is your life, and I'm not ready to hand that job to something that's never been scared. That's what I'd want people to understand.

headlineQuote: In live-line work, the man on the ground watching you is your life, and I'm not ready to hand that job to something that's never been scared.
portrait: Hana Dubois is a 43-year-old live-line specialist based at a market-town depot who also teaches apprentices two evenings a week, married to a baker, with two daughters and part-ownership of the bakery building. She's careful, devout and quietly warm, and uses AI now and then once others have shown it works. She stays calm in the hype and gradual scenarios, becomes anxious when AGI arrives in two years because both her pay and the bakery depend on the town, and settles into uneasy planning with more warning. Her path forward is full-time teaching and helping shape new apprenticeships. She blames reckless companies and leans on family and parish rather than government.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because both her income and the bakery's depend on the town being able to pay.
whatWouldHelp: The utility keeping experienced people on to train and supervise, funded colleges teaching new skills, and companies held back from moving faster than families can follow.
